destination.title: The FBI taped a microphone to a phone booth roof

short26: The FBI recorded every word he said — and never opened the door.
The Court still called it an illegal search.
Charles Katz stepped into a glass phone booth to place illegal betting calls.
To catch him, agents taped a hidden microphone to the outside of the glass, and never set foot inside.
For nearly forty years, the rule was simple: no physical trespass, no search.
But Katz had shut the door and paid the toll — to keep his words private, not his face.
The Fourth Amendment protects people, not places.
Recording him without a warrant was unconstitutional — not a ban on wiretaps, just a judge's permission first.
Justice Harlan's concurrence gave the reasonable-expectation-of-privacy test that still governs surveillance today.
Watch the full story on the channel.

candidate_payload_lines: Harlan's phrase — a "reasonable expectation of privacy" — was only one justice's gloss in 1967.
"The Fourth Amendment protects people, not places." What a person knowingly exposes to the public, even in his own home, is not protected.
The Fourth Amendment, he pointed out, protects "persons, houses, papers, and effects" against search and seizure — tangible things you can point to and carry away .
Your home, your papers, your property — the government could not come in and search them without a warrant.
In Los Angeles, in 1965, he was running a betting operation — taking wagers and passing gambling information over the phone .
So they tried something the law had never squarely tested.
The rule came from a 1928 case called Olmstead.
If the government can record you there simply because it never touched the walls, then your privacy hangs on a technicality — on where a microphone sits, not on what you reasonably expected .
Yet what Katz wanted to keep private was never how he looked.
A clever piece of surveillance that broke no rule because nobody trespassed — or a search of a private conversation, dressed up as something else ?
On December 18, 1967, the Supreme Court gave its answer — seven justices to one .
It no longer mattered that the agents had never physically entered the booth.
They never carried their evidence to a judge and asked permission before they began to listen .
It did not tell the government it could never record a suspect .
The agents outside never touched him, never stepped in, never broke a single thing .

shorts.angle: The one justice who dissented argued that a spoken sentence cannot be seized, and that rewriting the Fourth Amendment was Congress's job.
shorts.avoids: The existing Short names the seven to one vote and Harlan's concurrence but never says what the single dissenter thought; this cut is his argument.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: If the Constitution's words never mention conversations, where did the Court find the authority to protect them?

lines.text: One justice dissented in the case that gave you a right to privacy. His argument was the plain words on the page.
source_lines: One justice was not persuaded.

lines.text: Justice Hugo Black dissented alone. The Fourth Amendment, he pointed out, protects persons, houses, papers, and effects against search and seizure.
source_lines: Justice Hugo Black dissented, alone
The Fourth Amendment, he pointed out, protects "persons, houses, papers, and effects" against search and seizure

lines.text: Tangible things you can point to and carry away. A spoken conversation is none of those. You cannot seize a sentence.
source_lines: tangible things you can point to and carry away

lines.text: To Black, the majority was not so much reading the Constitution as quietly rewriting it. And rewriting it was Congress's job, not the Court's.
source_lines: To Black, the majority was not so much reading the Constitution as quietly rewriting it — and rewriting it was Congress's job, not the Court's

lines.text: The rule came from a 1928 case called Olmstead. Federal agents tapped a bootlegger's phone lines from the street, without ever entering his house.
source_lines: The rule came from a 1928 case called Olmstead.
Federal agents there had tapped a bootlegger's phone lines, but they did the tapping from wires out on the street, without ever entering his house.

lines.text: The Supreme Court said that was fine. No trespass into a protected place meant no search, and for decades the test stayed almost mechanical.
source_lines: The Supreme Court said that was fine: no trespass into a protected place meant no search
For decades, the test stayed almost mechanical.

lines.text: The majority's move was to stop asking where the government was standing and start asking what the person reasonably expected.
source_lines: Stop asking where the government was standing; start asking what the person reasonably expected.

lines.text: Seven justices went the other way. The trespass rule that had stood for nearly forty years was gone, and Black's plain words lost.

shorts.loop_join: L5 gives the outcome, Black beaten seven to one, so L1's 'one justice dissented' is heard again already knowing he was overruled.

shorts.angle: Katz anchored your privacy to what society is still prepared to accept as reasonable, so it shrinks every time being watched becomes more normal.
shorts.avoids: The existing Short presents Harlan's test as the settled standard that governs surveillance today; this cut is the weakness built into that standard.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: Whose expectations does a judge actually measure when he decides what society finds reasonable?

lines.text: The test that decides whether police need a warrant to track you is not fixed. It moves. And it has been moving.
source_lines: By anchoring privacy to what society thinks is reasonable, the Court made the Fourth Amendment flexible enough to follow new technology.

lines.text: Harlan's phrase, a reasonable expectation of privacy, was only one justice's gloss in 1967. Courts reached for it until it became the standard.
source_lines: Harlan's phrase — a "reasonable expectation of privacy" — was only one justice's gloss in 1967.
But in the years that followed, courts reached for it again and again, until it became the standard test for what even counts as a search

lines.text: When judges today ask whether police need a warrant to track your phone, read your messages, or follow your car, they are asking Harlan's question.
source_lines: When judges today ask whether the police need a warrant to track your phone, read your messages, or follow your car, they are usually asking Harlan's question

lines.text: But reasonable is a moving target. The more ordinary it becomes to be watched, the weaker anyone's claim that a given expectation still holds.
source_lines: But "reasonable" is a moving target. The more ordinary it becomes to be watched, the weaker anyone's claim that a given expectation still holds

lines.text: Harlan's test has two parts. A person must genuinely expect privacy, and that expectation must be one society is prepared to accept as reasonable.
source_lines: First, a person has to genuinely expect privacy.
Second, that expectation has to be one society is prepared to accept as reasonable

lines.text: The Court also drew a limit: what a person knowingly exposes to the public, even at home, is not protected.
source_lines: What a person knowingly exposes to the public, even in his own home, is not protected.

lines.text: Katz freed privacy from the walls, and tied it instead to what we are still willing to expect.
source_lines: Katz freed privacy from the walls — and tied it, instead, to what we are still willing to expect

lines.text: So the privacy you have tomorrow depends on how much watching we get used to today. Which way is that going?
